content.thinking:
I need to avoid citing precise figures and instead describe things relatively, like "several times baseline." The error rate only rose slightly above baseline, which wasn't the real signal—the latency series was what triggered the alert, even though the alert itself referenced error rate. The actual symptom users experienced was that shop pages responded slowly, so I need to trace the causal chain from there.

The sequence runs: latency spiked while CPU pinned at its limit, driven by a multi-fold surge in request volume starting around 07:35, hitting a fixed three-replica capacity that was never resized to match the new load—and the root cause of that traffic surge remains unknown, so I should stop speculating there. I'm also noticing a timing wrinkle: recovery appears to have started before the scale-out finished, meaning the fix might not have directly caused the recovery—traffic could have just dropped on its own—so I need to flag that as an assumption rather than state it as certain.

Disconnect logs show occurrences but nothing tying them clearly to the cause beyond likely client timeouts on slow pages. The lack of autoscaling or capacity headroom stands out as a contributing factor worth a new action item, and the alert that eventually fired came in quite late relative to when the issue actually started, which points to a detection gap needing its own action item—plus the alert itself seems mislabeled as an error-rate alert when the real signal was latency.

I should avoid citing exact timestamps, specific replica counts, or precise percentages, and instead use general phrasing like "its fixed replica count" or references to when the incident began.

action_items.item: Configure autoscaling for io-shop on CPU utilisation and request rate, with a replica ceiling and enough headroom to absorb a several-fold traffic increase. Review the per-replica CPU limit against current peak load.

Add alerts on sustained CPU use near the limit and on abnormal request-volume growth for io-shop, so the team is paged before latency degrades. Fix the HighLatency alert's description so it matches the series it evaluates.

Find the source of the traffic increase from edge and access logs, such as a campaign, a partner, a crawler or a bot. Record whether it is expected to recur and whether rate limiting or capacity planning needs to account for it.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow io-shop pages and a slightly higher share of failed requests. The latency series behind the alert went from {series_before} before onset to {series_while_broken} on average, peaking at {series_at_worst}. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken}, peaking at {errors_at_worst}.
Latency at the median and the tail rose far above baseline because the service's CPU was pinned at its configured limit, so requests queued instead of being served promptly.
CPU use climbed in step with a sustained, several-fold rise in request volume that began well before the latency blow-up. The traffic outgrew what the replicas could serve.

The capacity did not change as load grew. The CPU limit stayed fixed for the whole window and the replicas stayed as they were, until Argus scaled the deployment out. No deploy, release or flag change was recorded that could explain the onset, so this was a demand problem and not a code or config regression.

contributing_factors.factor: Capacity was static. Nothing added replicas or CPU when traffic rose several-fold, so a load increase went straight into CPU saturation.

Detection was late. The alert was raised at {alert_raised}, long after the onset at {began} and at about the time the metrics show recovery. Nothing flagged the traffic climb or the CPU approaching its limit while there was still headroom. The alert is also named for error rate while the series it evaluates is latency, which makes it confusing to triage.
The pull request proposed by the Code-Fix Agent addresses a capacity incident in which no code change was involved. It is not clear that it is relevant, and it remains open.
The source of the traffic surge was never established, so the team cannot tell whether it was organic, a campaign, or abusive or automated traffic.

input.executive_summary: For about {duration}, from {began} to {recovered}, the io-shop storefront was slow, and a small extra share of requests failed (error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}). Shoppers were affected across the service. Traffic had grown several times over its normal level and the service did not have enough CPU to keep up. No deploy, config or flag change was involved. Argus scaled the service out, and the metrics were back at baseline soon after. The metrics show recovery from {recovered}, which is before the scale-out was issued, so traffic may have eased on its own. The cause of the traffic surge is not known.

got_lucky: The metrics show the service back at baseline from {recovered}, before the scale-out was issued. The surge may have eased by itself, so the scale-out may not be what ended it. If the traffic had stayed high, impact would have lasted until the scale-out landed.
went_well: Argus picked up the alert within seconds, read the metrics, changes, flags and logs, and correctly identified demand saturation from the traffic and CPU series.
The scale-out was a low-risk action that matched the diagnosis, and Argus verified it against the paging rule before declaring the incident mitigated.
went_wrong: The alert fired long after the onset, so most of the degradation passed before anyone was engaged.
Capacity did not respond to the load increase on its own.
Argus's logs held only client-disconnect and error-rate lines, which did not point to the cause. The diagnosis rested on metrics alone.

input.root_cause: io-shop ran on a fixed set of replicas, each with a fixed CPU limit, sized for the old traffic level. When request volume rose several-fold, CPU pinned at that limit and latency rose sharply. Nothing added capacity automatically.
input.symptom: Shop pages were slow and some requests failed
